ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Nursing, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, approved the protocol (No.
01, 16 September 2025), and the study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2025).
Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older who resided in Greece and could read and understand Greek.

Participants were asked how often they simultaneously use social media on their smartphone (e.g., scrolling through feeds, communicating with friends, browsing posts or videos) for reasons unrelated to the content being watched, when watching a movie, TV series, sports event, or other content on any device (e.g., TV, computer, tablet) either alone or together with other people.
Detailed characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We calculated the required sample size for the multiple linear regression models, which included five independent variables. To detect a small effect size (f² = 0.02) for each independent variable, with a significance level of 0.05 and statistical power of 95%, the minimum required sample size was 652 participants. For the comparison of content-unrelated social media second-screen use between solitary viewing and coviewing, the minimum required sample size to detect a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.2) with the same significance level and power was 327 participants. Our sample of 922 participants exceeded both requirements, yielding a statistical power of 99% to detect a small effect size for each independent variable in the multiple linear regression models. Sample size and power were calculated with the noncentral F and t distributions.

text.text: Background: Research on second screening has focused mainly on content-related activities, such as discussing a programme on social media, whereas social media use that is unrelated to the content being watched has received little attention.

Aim: We examined the frequency of content-unrelated social media second-screen use during solitary viewing and co-viewing, and its associations with sex, age, problematic social media use, fear of missing out and loneliness.
Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey with 922 adults in Greece from June to November 2026.
Content-unrelated social media second-screen use during solitary viewing and co-viewing was measured with two single items on an 11-point scale.
We used the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, the three-item UCLA Loneliness Scale and a single item on fear of missing out.
We performed the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and simple and multiple linear regression analyses, and we used ordinal logistic regression as a sensitivity analysis.
Results: Overall, 91.0% of participants reported content-unrelated social media second-screen use during solitary viewing and 79.6% during co-viewing.
This behaviour was more frequent during solitary viewing than during co-viewing (mean = 4.65 vs.

In multiple regression analyses, higher levels of problematic social media use (β = 0.23 for solitary viewing and 0.28 for co-viewing) and fear of missing out (β = 0.22 for both contexts) were associated with more frequent use in both viewing contexts.
Female sex (β = 0.09) and younger age (β = -0.15) were associated with more frequent use only during solitary viewing.
Loneliness was associated with content-unrelated social media second-screen use in simple analyses, but not after adjustment.
The sensitivity analysis yielded the same conclusions.
Conclusions: Content-unrelated social media second-screen use is very common and is more frequent during solitary viewing.

Problematic social media use and fear of missing out are the main correlates of this behaviour, which seems to reflect a vulnerability to compulsive social media engagement shaped by the social context of viewing.
Longitudinal studies with representative samples are needed to confirm our findings.
The simultaneous use of a second digital device while watching audiovisual content has become a routine feature of contemporary media consumption.

In the communication literature, this behaviour has been described as second screening, that is, the use of a smartphone, tablet or laptop while watching television in order to access the Internet and social network sites (Gil de Zúñiga et al., 2015).

text.text: To date, research on second screening has been dominated by a content-related perspective.

Most studies have conceptualised the second screen as an extension of the viewing experience, through which viewers seek additional information about the programme, discuss it with others, or share their reactions in real time (Gil de Zúñiga et al., 2015; Guo, 2019).

text.text: This perspective underlies research on social television, which has examined the motives and antecedents of programme-related interaction on social media.

In this line of research, the frequency of social television use has been associated with communication, information and entertainment motives and with perceived social gratifications (Habes et al., 2025; Krämer et al., 2015), as well as with programme affinity, interpersonal interaction and the perceived characteristics of second-screen platforms (Guo, 2019).

text.text: Similarly, complementary second-screen use has been linked to greater engagement with television content (Nee & Dozier, 2017), and studies of televised sport have identified fan passion, fear of missing out and demographic characteristics as correlates of second-screen use during matches (Çelik & Şirin, 2023; Galily et al., 2024).

text.text: Consequently, the second screen has been examined predominantly as a complement to, rather than a competitor of, the content being watched.
The literature on content-unrelated social media second-screen use is very limited.

Among university students in Türkiye, communicating with friends and following social media accounts were among the most frequently endorsed reasons for using a second screen during television viewing, alongside relieving boredom and having fun (Yeşilyurt & Karaduman, 2025).

Where content-unrelated activities have been measured, they have usually been examined as a secondary outcome within studies of specific media events, mainly live sport, and with measures that combine social media use with other online activities, such as general Internet browsing (Elishar-Malka et al., 2021; Weimann-Saks et al., 2024).

text.text: Moreover, existing studies have typically focused on a single broadcast or programme genre, rather than on habitual behaviour across different types of content and viewing devices.
As a result, little is known about how often individuals use social media for reasons unrelated to the content they are watching, or about the factors that predict this behaviour.

text.text: These findings suggest that content-unrelated second screening operates as a competing activity that diverts attention from the primary content, rather than as an enhancement of the viewing experience.
The social context of viewing is also likely to be relevant.
Television viewing has increasingly become a solitary activity (Krämer et al., 2015).

text.text: During solitary viewing, social media may offer opportunities for social connection to viewers who are physically alone (Krämer et al., 2015; Nee & Barker, 2020), and research on sport viewing suggests that unmarried viewers, who are more likely to watch alone, engage more frequently in second screening (Galily et al., 2024).

text.text: During co-viewing, in contrast, content-unrelated social media use may withdraw attention not only from the content but also from the people with whom the content is being watched.

This behaviour resembles phubbing, that is, ignoring co-present others in favour of one's smartphone, which has been associated with problematic smartphone use and fear of missing out (Ansari et al., 2024; Chotpitayasunondh & Douglas, 2016), whereas being phubbed has been associated with adverse emotional and relational consequences (Nuñez & Radtke, 2024).

text.text: Therefore, the frequency and predictors of content-unrelated social media second-screen use may differ between solitary viewing and co-viewing.
To the best of our knowledge, however, no study has compared content-unrelated social media second-screen use across these two viewing contexts.
Several individual characteristics may account for differences in content-unrelated social media second-screen use.
Findings on sex and age have been inconsistent.

Among university students, females were more likely than males to use a second screen to follow their social media accounts and to message friends while watching television (Yeşilyurt & Karaduman, 2025), and covert observation showed that females looked away from the main screen for longer than males (Noschang, 2026).

text.text: Thus, the roles of sex and age in content-unrelated social media second-screen use remain unclear.
Two theoretical frameworks are particularly relevant for explaining individual differences in content-unrelated social media second-screen use.

According to the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, addictive patterns of internet use develop through the interaction of predisposing personal characteristics with affective and cognitive responses to situational triggers, in combination with reduced executive control (Brand et al., 2016 (Brand et al., , 2019)).

text.text: Within this framework, viewing situations may act as triggers for habitual social media checking, particularly among individuals with problematic social media use and high fear of missing out.

In contrast, the model of compensatory internet use proposes that individuals go online to escape real-life problems or to alleviate negative moods, and that motivations mediate the relationship between psychosocial well-being and problematic internet use (Kardefelt-Winther, 2014).

text.text: From this perspective, lonely individuals may use social media during viewing to compensate for a lack of social contact, although the association between loneliness and this behaviour may be indirect.
Psychological factors may provide a more consistent explanation.
Loneliness may motivate individuals to turn to social media in order to obtain social contact during viewing, particularly when they watch alone (Galily et al., 2024; Krämer et al., 2015).

text.text: Consistent with this, a meta-analysis of 133 studies found moderate positive correlations between problematic social media use and loneliness (Huang, 2022).

text.text: Problematic social media use, which involves excessive use that individuals find difficult to control, may also render social media use during viewing habitual and independent of the content being watched.

Fear of missing out, defined as a pervasive apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences from which one is absent, is accompanied by a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing (Przybylski et al., 2013).

text.text: Fear of missing out is strongly associated with problematic social media use (Du et al., 2024; Montag et al., 2023), has predicted second-screen use among sports fans (Çelik & Şirin, 2023), and has been linked to phubbing through smartphone addiction (Chotpitayasunondh & Douglas, 2016).

text.text: However, to the best of our knowledge, no study has examined whether loneliness, problematic social media use and fear of missing out are associated with contentunrelated social media second-screen use, or whether these associations differ between solitary viewing and co-viewing.

To address these gaps, the present study examined content-unrelated social media second-screen use, defined as the use of social media on a smartphone (e.g., scrolling through feeds, communicating with friends, browsing posts or videos) for reasons unrelated to the content being watched, while simultaneously watching a movie, TV series, sports event, or other content on another device.

In particular, the aims of the study were (a) to estimate the frequency of content-unrelated social media secondscreen use during solitary viewing and during co-viewing among adults in Greece; (b) to compare the frequency of this behaviour between the two viewing contexts; and (c) to examine the associations of sex, age, problematic social media use, fear of missing out and loneliness with content-unrelated social media second-screen use in each viewing context.

text.text: On the basis of the evidence reviewed above, we formulated the following hypotheses.
H1: We hypothesised that content-unrelated social media second-screen use would be more frequent during solitary viewing than during co-viewing.
H2: We hypothesised that sex would be associated with content-unrelated social media second-screen use during both solitary viewing and co-viewing.
H3: We hypothesised that age would be associated with content-unrelated social media second-screen use during both solitary viewing and co-viewing.

H4: We hypothesised that higher levels of problematic social media use would be associated with more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use during both solitary viewing and co-viewing.
H5: We hypothesised that higher levels of fear of missing out would be associated with more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use during both solitary viewing and co-viewing.
H6: We hypothesised that higher levels of loneliness would be associated with more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use during both solitary viewing and co-viewing.
Because previous findings on sex and age have been inconsistent, H2 and H3 were non-directional.
This was a cross-sectional survey carried out in Greece from June to November 2026.

Respondents completed an anonymous questionnaire hosted on Google Forms, which was promoted through posts on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn; recruitment therefore relied on convenience sampling.

Because the behaviour of interest takes place online, an internet survey reached the relevant population efficiently, and completing the questionnaire privately and at one's own pace was expected to encourage honest reporting.
Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older who resided in Greece and could read and understand Greek.
Before data collection, we conducted a pilot study with 20 participants, using cognitive interviews to assess whether the items were clear and understandable.
Participants reported no difficulties or questions, and therefore no modifications were needed.
Completion of the questionnaire required approximately 5 minutes.
All items were mandatory, so there were no missing data.
The final sample comprised 922 participants.

For the comparison of content-unrelated social media second-screen use between solitary viewing and coviewing, the minimum required sample size to detect a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.2) with the same significance level and power was 327 participants.
Our sample of 922 participants exceeded both requirements, yielding a statistical power of 99% to detect a small effect size for each independent variable in the multiple linear regression models.

Participants reported their sex (male or female) and age (in years).
We assessed content-unrelated social media second-screen use with two single items developed for the present study, referring to solitary viewing and co-viewing, respectively.

Participants were asked how often they simultaneously use social media on their smartphone (e.g., scrolling through feeds, communicating with friends, browsing posts or videos) for reasons unrelated to the content being watched, when watching a movie, TV series, sports event, or other content on any device (e.g., TV, computer, tablet) either alone or together with other people.
Responses were recorded on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (never) to 10 (always), with higher scores indicating more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use.
No recall period was specified; thus, the items captured habitual behaviour.

To examine the associations of sex, age, problematic social media use, fear of missing out and loneliness with content-unrelated social media second-screen use (H2-H6), we first performed simple linear regression analyses for each independent variable.
Then, to examine independent associations, we constructed multiple linear regression models in which all independent variables were entered simultaneously.
Separate models were constructed for solitary viewing and co-viewing.
We report unstandardised coefficients (b) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), standardised coefficients (β) and p-values.
Because the Breusch-Pagan test indicated heteroscedasticity, we used heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors.

Normality of residuals was assessed with skewness and kurtosis values (absolute values ≤ 0.52 in both models), and independence of errors with the Durbin-Watson statistic (1.76 and 1.90 for solitary viewing and co-viewing, respectively).
Multicollinearity was assessed with the variance inflation factor (VIF); all VIF values were below 1.6.
No influential observations were identified (maximum Cook's distance = 0.03).

Because the dependent variables were measured on 11-point scales, we performed a sensitivity analysis in which the multiple linear regression models were repeated as ordinal logistic regression models (proportional odds models), treating the 11 response categories as ordered; we report unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs from simple and multiple ordinal logistic regression models.
The proportional odds assumption was examined by comparing the ORs obtained from cumulative binary logistic regression models at different cut-points.

To test whether the associations of the independent variables differed between the two viewing contexts, we fitted a pooled model in long format that included viewing context, the five independent variables and the context-by-variable interaction terms, with robust standard errors clustered by participant.
P-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine content-unrelated social media second-screen use as a distinct behaviour, to compare it between solitary viewing and co-viewing, and to investigate its predictors.
We found that contentunrelated social media second-screen use was highly prevalent, since 91.0% of participants reported such use during solitary viewing and 79.6% during co-viewing.
This behaviour was considerably more frequent during solitary viewing than during co-viewing.

Problematic social media use and fear of missing out were independently associated with more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use in both viewing contexts, whereas female sex and younger age were associated with more frequent use only during solitary viewing.
Loneliness was associated with content-unrelated social media second-screen use in simple analyses, but this association disappeared after adjustment for the other variables.
These findings were robust in a sensitivity analysis with ordinal logistic regression.
The high prevalence of content-unrelated social media second-screen use suggests that, for most adults, watching audiovisual content is no longer an activity that receives undivided attention.

This finding complements previous research, which has focused mainly on content-related second screening, such as seeking additional information about the programme or discussing it on social media (Gil de Zúñiga et al., 2015; Guo, 2019; Krämer et al., 2015).

text.text: Our results are consistent with survey data indicating that most online activity during television viewing is unrelated to the programme (Krämer et al., 2015), and with observational evidence showing that viewers frequently look away from the main screen and underestimate this behaviour in self-reports (Noschang, 2026).

text.text: Previous studies have shown that content-unrelated second screening is negatively associated with engagement, enjoyment and transportation during live sport (Elishar-Malka et al., 2021; Weimann-Saks et al., 2024) and with less favourable attitudes towards the programme (Gelper et al., 2025).

text.text: Therefore, content-unrelated social media second-screen use should be considered a competing activity that fragments attention, rather than an extension of the viewing experience.
As we hypothesised, content-unrelated social media second-screen use was more frequent during solitary viewing than during co-viewing, and the difference was substantial (r = 0.60; Cohen's d = 0.57).

A plausible explanation is that solitary viewing lacks the social interaction that accompanies co-viewing, so viewers who watch alone may turn to social media to obtain social contact and stimulation (Krämer et al., 2015; Nee & Barker, 2020).
text.formatted: A plausible explanation is that solitary viewing lacks the social interaction that accompanies co-viewing, so viewers who watch alone may turn to social media to obtain social contact and stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Krämer et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Nee & Barker, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the physical presence of other people may provide social interaction directly and may also impose social norms that discourage individuals from turning to their smartphones, since such behaviour may be perceived as phubbing (Chotpitayasunondh & Douglas, 2016).
text.formatted: In contrast, the physical presence of other people may provide social interaction directly and may also impose social norms that discourage individuals from turning to their smartphones, since such behaviour may be perceived as phubbing <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chotpitayasunondh & Douglas, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, approximately four in five participants reported content-unrelated social media use even during co-viewing, which suggests that smartphone use in the presence of others has become largely normative.

Moreover, the strong correlation between the two viewing contexts indicates that content-unrelated social media second-screen use reflects a relatively stable individual tendency, the expression of which is shaped by the social context of viewing.
Problematic social media use and fear of missing out were the strongest correlates of content-unrelated social media second-screen use, and their associations were similar in both viewing contexts.

These findings are in line with the definition of fear of missing out as an apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences, which is accompanied by a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing (Przybylski et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These findings are in line with the definition of fear of missing out as an apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences, which is accompanied by a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Przybylski et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with high levels of fear of missing out may therefore find it difficult to disconnect from social media even while watching a movie or a sports event.
Our findings extend previous evidence showing that fear of missing out predicts second-screen use among sports fans (Çelik & Şirin, 2023) to contentunrelated use across different types of content.
text.formatted: Our findings extend previous evidence showing that fear of missing out predicts second-screen use among sports fans <ref type="bibr">(Çelik & Şirin, 2023)</ref> to contentunrelated use across different types of content.

text.text: Similarly, problematic social media use is characterised by excessive and poorly controlled use, which may render social media checking habitual and independent of the content being watched.

Since fear of missing out and problematic social media use are strongly correlated (Du et al., 2024; Montag et al., 2023), both variables may reflect a broader vulnerability to compulsive social media engagement.

text.text: The fact that their associations did not differ between solitary viewing and co-viewing suggests that this vulnerability operates regardless of the presence of other people.

These findings are consistent with the I-PACE model, according to which situational triggers elicit habitual responses among individuals with a predisposition to addictive internet use (Brand et al., 2016 (Brand et al., , 2019)).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with the I-PACE model, according to which situational triggers elicit habitual responses among individuals with a predisposition to addictive internet use <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brand et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brand et al., , 2019))</ref>.

text.text: Contrary to our hypothesis, loneliness was not independently associated with contentunrelated social media second-screen use.
Loneliness was positively associated with this behaviour in simple analyses, but its coefficient decreased by more than 75% after adjustment and was no longer statistically significant.
A likely explanation is the overlap between loneliness, problematic social media use and fear of missing out.
In our study, loneliness was positively correlated with both variables, and a meta-analysis has shown moderate positive correlations between problematic social media use and loneliness (Huang, 2022).
text.formatted: In our study, loneliness was positively correlated with both variables, and a meta-analysis has shown moderate positive correlations between problematic social media use and loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Huang, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, lonely individuals may engage more frequently in content-unrelated social media second-screen use because they are more prone to problematic social media use and fear of missing out, rather than because of loneliness per se.

This interpretation is in line with the model of compensatory internet use, which proposes that psychosocial problems such as loneliness are associated with problematic internet use mainly indirectly, through motivations and coping processes (Kardefelt-Winther, 2014).
text.formatted: This interpretation is in line with the model of compensatory internet use, which proposes that psychosocial problems such as loneliness are associated with problematic internet use mainly indirectly, through motivations and coping processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kardefelt-Winther, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, the cross-sectional design of our study did not allow us to test this indirect pathway, which should be examined in future longitudinal studies with mediation analysis.
Sex and age were associated with content-unrelated social media second-screen use only during solitary viewing, and the differences between the two viewing contexts were statistically significant.
During solitary viewing, females and younger adults reported more frequent use.

These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that females were more likely than males to use a second screen to follow social media accounts and to message friends while watching television (Yeşilyurt & Karaduman, 2025), and that females looked away from the main screen for longer than males (Noschang, 2026).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that females were more likely than males to use a second screen to follow social media accounts and to message friends while watching television <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Yeşilyurt & Karaduman, 2025)</ref>, and that females looked away from the main screen for longer than males <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Noschang, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, studies of televised sport have found that second screening is more common among males and older viewers (Galily et al., 2024), which suggests that demographic differences depend on the type of content and on whether second screening is related to the content.

text.text: During co-viewing, the associations of sex and age disappeared after adjustment, which suggests that the social context of coviewing may attenuate demographic differences in content-unrelated social media second-screen use.
When other people are present, social norms regarding smartphone use may apply similarly to all viewers, regardless of their sex and age.
Our findings have several practical implications.

First, since problematic social media use and fear of missing out were the most important correlates of content-unrelated social media second-screen use, interventions that aim to reduce problematic social media use and fear of missing out may also help individuals to watch audiovisual content with undivided attention.

Second, health professionals and educators could include content-unrelated second-screen use in digital literacy and digital well-being programmes, by raising awareness of how habitual social media checking fragments attention during leisure activities.

Third, the lower frequency of content-unrelated social media second-screen use during co-viewing suggests that shared viewing may limit this behaviour, which could be considered in recommendations for healthy media use.
Our study has several limitations.
First, we used a cross-sectional design, and therefore we cannot infer causal relationships between the independent variables and contentunrelated social media second-screen use.
For example, frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use may also reinforce problematic social media use and fear of missing out.
Second, we used a convenience sample recruited through social media, in which females (79.3%) and younger adults (median age = 23 years) were overrepresented.
Therefore, our results may not be generalisable to the general population, and the findings regarding older adults should be interpreted with caution.
Moreover, no technical measure was used to prevent multiple submissions by the same individual.

Third, all variables were self-reported, and observational evidence shows that self-reports underestimate multitasking during viewing (Noschang, 2026); therefore, the frequency of content-unrelated social media second-screen use may have been underestimated.
text.formatted: Third, all variables were self-reported, and observational evidence shows that self-reports underestimate multitasking during viewing <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Noschang, 2026)</ref>; therefore, the frequency of content-unrelated social media second-screen use may have been underestimated.

text.text: Fourth, we measured content-unrelated social media secondscreen use and fear of missing out with single items that had not been previously validated, and the items did not specify a recall period.
Moreover, the items described activities rather than specific platforms, and participants may have differed in whether they considered messaging applications as social media.
Fifth, we did not measure content-related second-screen use, and therefore we could not compare the predictors of content-related and content-unrelated use.

Sixth, we did not assess the type of content (e.g., movies, series, sports events), the viewing device or the duration of viewing, which may influence content-unrelated social media second-screen use.

In addition, we did not measure marital status, living arrangements or overall time spent on social media, which may have confounded the observed associations; for example, unmarried individuals and those who live alone may watch content alone more often (Galily et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In addition, we did not measure marital status, living arrangements or overall time spent on social media, which may have confounded the observed associations; for example, unmarried individuals and those who live alone may watch content alone more often <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Galily et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our study was conducted in Greece, and cultural differences in media use and in norms regarding smartphone use during co-viewing may limit the generalisability of our findings to other countries.

Future studies should use longitudinal designs to examine the temporal relationships between problematic social media use, fear of missing out, loneliness and contentunrelated social media second-screen use, and to test whether problematic social media use and fear of missing out mediate the association between loneliness and this behaviour.
Experience sampling and mobile diary methods (Gelper et al., 2025), as well as objective smartphone use data, could provide more accurate estimates than retrospective self-reports.
text.formatted: Experience sampling and mobile diary methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gelper et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as objective smartphone use data, could provide more accurate estimates than retrospective self-reports.

text.text: Moreover, the psychometric properties of the single items used in our study should be examined in further studies, and multi-item scales for content-unrelated social media second-screen use should be developed.

Future studies should also measure content-related and content-unrelated second-screen use simultaneously, examine the role of content type and viewing device, and include representative samples from different countries.
Content-unrelated social media second-screen use was very common among adults in Greece and was more frequent during solitary viewing than during co-viewing.

Problematic social media use and fear of missing out were associated with more frequent content-unrelated social media second-screen use in both viewing contexts, whereas female sex and younger age were associated with more frequent use only during solitary viewing.
Loneliness was not independently associated with this behaviour.

Our findings suggest that content-unrelated social media second-screen use is a distinct form of media multitasking that is driven mainly by a vulnerability to compulsive social media engagement and is shaped by the social context of viewing.
Further longitudinal studies with representative samples are needed to confirm our findings.
